sentences.text: Sinosaurus shares a similar cranial crest shape with Dilophosaurus, though its exact taxonomic relationship remains uncertain.
A nearly complete skull measures 51.96 centimeters in total length and is similar in size to that of Dilophosaurus.
Although Sinosaurus possessed dual crests, research found these structures could not be used for combat.
The type species Sinosaurus triassicus was named by Chung Chieng Young in 1940.
The type specimen was recovered from the Zhangjiawa Member of the Lufeng Formation in Yunnan, China.
Dong (2003) proposed that a deep notch in the skull housed jaw muscles, giving Sinosaurus a powerful bite.
Based on jaw power estimates, Sinosaurus might have been either a carnivore or a scavenger.
The species S. sinensis was originally assigned to Dilophosaurus before being reassigned to Sinosaurus.
The species Shuangbaisaurus anlongbaoensis has been considered a synonym of Sinosaurus triassicus.
In 2003, Oliver Rauhut classified Sinosaurus as an advanced theropod related to Cryolophosaurus and Dilophosaurus sinensis.
Fossils of Sinosaurus have been found in the Lufeng Formation in Yunnan Province, China.

Sinosaurus lived during the Sinemurian stage of the Jurassic period, approximately 196 to 183 million years ago, though other estimates suggest it lived from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian stages between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago, or from the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages approximately 196 to 189 million years ago.
Sinosaurus shared its environment with therapsids, archosaurs, diapsids, crocodylomorphs, and early mammals in the Lufeng Formation.
Wang et al. (2017) argued that Dilophosaurus sinensis may be distinct from Sinosaurus triassicus based on differences in premaxilla anatomy.
It is debated whether Changpeipus footprints from the Lufeng Formation were made by Sinosaurus or Coelophysis sp.
Wang et al. (2026) described a new theropod distinct from Sinosaurus with tetanuran-like characters and named the new clade Averostriformes.
